1.title: Sunday Lunch at the Ospinas'
paragraphs: Every Sunday at about one o'clock, the narrow street outside the Ospina family's house in Envigado fills up with cars. Aunts arrive carrying pots of beans, cousins bring bags of arepas, and somebody always forgets the ice. By two o'clock there are usually more than twenty people sitting at three tables pushed together in the garden. "Nobody sends an invitation," says Gloria Ospina, who is seventy-four and has hosted the lunch for almost four decades. "The rule is that if you are family, you come."

Sociologists often describe Colombian families as close-knit, and the Ospinas seem to prove the point. Three generations live within ten minutes of one another, and most important decisions, from buying a car to choosing a university, are discussed around Gloria's table. Her grandson Mateo, who is nineteen, admits that this can be exhausting. "Being part of a big family means never being able to keep a secret," he says. "If I tell my mum something on Friday, my great-aunt knows about it by Sunday."

Even so, Mateo says he enjoys spending time with his relatives, and he can't imagine skipping the lunch. He gets along especially well with his uncle Hernán, the family's self-declared black sheep, who left a stable job in a bank to open a surf school on the Pacific coast. "Everyone criticised him at first," Mateo recalls. "Now they all ask him for holiday discounts." Several people say that Mateo takes after Hernán: both are easygoing, both hate wearing ties, and both keep making jokes during the speeches.

Of course, not every Sunday is peaceful. Two of Gloria's daughters stopped speaking to each other for nearly a year after a disagreement about an inheritance. "What upset me most was that they argued in front of the children," Gloria says. In the end, it was the lunch itself that helped them patch things up. "They couldn't avoid seeing each other, so eventually they had to start talking again."

Researchers who study family life point out that regular rituals like this one give people a sense of belonging, especially in times of change. Young adults who grow up with these traditions often report feeling more secure, even when they move away. The challenge, however, is that modern life makes the habit harder to keep. Jobs, traffic and long distances mean that many families now meet only at Christmas.

Gloria is aware that the tradition may not survive her. "My only worry is that nobody will want to cook for twenty people," she says with a smile. Mateo, listening nearby, has a different idea. "The solution is that we all cook a little," he says. "And Hernán buys the ice."

1.title: Can Siblings Really Be Friends?
paragraphs: Dr Paula Ríos is a family therapist in Bogotá and the author of a popular book about brothers and sisters. We asked her why sibling relationships can be so complicated, and what adults can do when they have drifted apart.

Q: Why do brothers and sisters fight so much when they are young? A: The simple answer is that they are competing for the same limited resources: their parents' attention, approval and time. Sibling rivalry is completely normal. What worries me is not arguing itself, but parents comparing their children all the time. Phrases like 'Why can't you be more like your sister?' can stay with a person for decades.

Q: Is it true that birth order shapes our personality? A: There's some evidence, but I'd take most popular theories with caution. Older children are often described as responsible and younger ones as rebellious, but family size, gender and economic situation matter just as much. The important thing is that every child feels seen for who they are.

Q: Many adults say they love their siblings but don't really like them. Is that common? A: Very. You don't choose your siblings, so it's natural that some of them rub you up the wrong way. You might share childhood memories but disagree about politics, religion or money. Lots of my clients say they simply don't see eye to eye with a brother or sister on anything important. That doesn't mean the relationship has failed.

Q: How do siblings drift apart? A: Usually it happens slowly. People move to different cities, have children, get busy. Then something happens, often when parents become ill or die, and old resentments come back. The danger is that nobody wants to be the first to apologise, so years go by without anyone picking up the phone.

Q: So what would you advise someone who wants to reconnect? A: Start small. Instead of planning a big conversation about the past, try suggesting a coffee or a short walk. Avoid bringing up old arguments in the first meeting. Focus on listening rather than proving you were right. Many people are surprised to discover that their sibling has also been missing them.

Q: And what can parents do to help their children bond? A: Give them shared projects rather than competitions: cooking a meal together, building something, looking after a pet. Children who learn to cooperate early are much more likely to keep in touch later. My own view is that a nurturing home isn't one without conflict. It's one where people learn how to repair things after a fight.

2.title: The Empty Lighthouse
paragraphs: On 26 December 1900, a supply ship called the Hesperus approached Eilean Mòr, a small rocky island in the Flannan Isles, off the north-west coast of Scotland. Its crew expected to see the three lighthouse keepers waiting at the landing, as they always did. Instead, there was nobody. No flag was flying, and the boxes that should have been ready for collection were missing. The silence was eerie.

A relief keeper named Joseph Moore climbed the steep path to the lighthouse. The gate and the door were closed, the beds were unmade and the kitchen clock had stopped. Two of the men's heavy waterproof coats were gone, but the third was still hanging on its hook. The keepers, James Ducat, Thomas Marshall and Donald MacArthur, were never seen again.

For more than a century, people have tried to figure out what happened. The investigators who arrived a few days later found important clues at the west landing, where a storm had clearly caused serious damage. Heavy equipment had been moved, and part of a railing had been torn away. Their conclusion was that the men must have gone down to secure their equipment during bad weather and been swept away by an unusually large wave.

That explanation sounds reasonable, but it doesn't explain everything. Why was one coat left behind? The rules were strict: one keeper had to stay inside the lighthouse at all times. If all three men went out, one of them must have broken the rules, perhaps because he saw his colleagues in danger and ran out to help them. Of course, he might simply have forgotten his coat in the panic.

Over the years, the story has attracted more imaginative theories. Some writers have suggested that the men might have been kidnapped by foreign spies, or that one keeper could have attacked the others and then thrown himself into the sea. Others have blamed ghosts or giant sea birds. Most historians say these ideas can't have much basis in fact, since there is no evidence to support them, only circumstantial details that have been exaggerated with each retelling.

In hindsight, it is easy to say that the keepers should have been more careful, or that the authorities should have built a safer landing. But the people who worked on these remote islands lived with danger every day. Perhaps the most sensible view is that the sea, which surrounded them constantly, finally took them. With so little evidence, however, we will probably never know for certain, and that is exactly why the mystery continues to fascinate.

2.title: The Day I Accused My Neighbour
paragraphs: I would like to say that I am a calm, reasonable person who never jumps to conclusions. Unfortunately, last March proved otherwise. This is the story of how I accused an innocent man of stealing my bicycle, in front of eighty people, and what I learned from it.

I live in a twelve-storey building in Laureles, Medellín, where I keep my bike in a small storage area next to the car park. One Monday morning I went down to get it and found only the lock, lying open on the floor. I was furious. That bike had cost me three months' savings, and I needed it to get to work.

My suspicions fell immediately on the new tenant in 7B, a quiet man in his forties who had moved in two weeks earlier. I had seen him in the car park late on Sunday night, carrying a large bag, and he hadn't said hello. In my head, the case was closed. He must have taken it, I thought. Who else could it have been?

So I did what many of us do now: I wrote a long message to the building's WhatsApp group. I didn't name him directly, but I mentioned "a new resident" and "suspicious behaviour on Sunday night". Within an hour, my neighbours had worked out who I meant. Some sent angry emojis; others suggested calling the police.

The real explanation arrived that afternoon, from Don Álvaro, the building's porter. Because of a water leak, the maintenance team had needed to empty the storage area over the weekend, so he had moved all the bikes to the basement. He had cut my lock because I hadn't left a key. The man in 7B, it turned out, had simply been taking his rubbish out.

With the benefit of hindsight, I can see all the things I should have done. I should have asked the porter first. I shouldn't have treated circumstantial details as proof. I needn't have written that message at all; a simple question would have solved the mystery in minutes. And I definitely should have apologised in person, rather than in the group, where my original message was still there for everyone to read.

In the end I knocked on his door with a box of buñuelos. His name is Ricardo, he works night shifts at a hospital, and he was much kinder about the whole thing than I deserved. Now, whenever I feel the urge to blame someone, I remember his face when he opened the door, and I ask one more question before I decide who the culprit is.

3.title: Barichara: Slow Travel in Stone
paragraphs: Arriving in Barichara after six hours on a bus from Bogotá feels a little like stepping into an old photograph. The streets, which are paved with large, uneven blocks of local sandstone, climb gently towards a cathedral of the same warm, golden colour. White houses with green doors and red-tiled roofs line every corner, and the only sound in the early afternoon is the occasional motorbike.

Barichara, which sits on a plateau in the department of Santander, is often described as the most beautiful small town in Colombia. It is certainly one of the best preserved. Founded in the eighteenth century, it is steeped in colonial history, and strict rules mean that new buildings must follow traditional styles. While larger towns nearby have filled with shopping centres and concrete apartment blocks, Barichara has kept its quaint, almost theatrical charm.

The town is only a stone's throw from San Gil, Colombia's adventure-sports capital, yet the atmosphere could hardly be more different. Whereas visitors to San Gil come for rafting, paragliding and caving, people who come to Barichara mostly want to slow down. The best way to soak up the atmosphere is simply to walk without a plan, stopping for a cold drink in one of the small squares or a coffee in a courtyard full of bougainvillea.

For something more active, the Camino Real is well worth a detour. This old stone path, which was used for centuries by indigenous Guane people and later by Spanish traders, winds for about nine kilometres down the canyon to the tiny village of Guane. The walk takes around two and a half hours. Although it is mostly downhill, the sun can be fierce, so it is a good idea to start early and carry plenty of water. Buses run back to Barichara a few times a day.

Barichara's popularity does have a downside. In recent years, boutique hotels and expensive restaurants have sprung up along the main streets, and some residents complain that property prices have risen beyond the reach of local families. On holiday weekends, the town can feel crowded. Despite this, it remains far quieter than most destinations on the tourist trail, and on a weekday evening you may have the viewpoint above the canyon almost to yourself.

If you only have time for one place in Santander, choose Barichara. Bring comfortable shoes, leave your schedule at home and give yourself at least two nights. The town rewards people who are not in a hurry.

3.title: Why I Swapped the Big City for a Small Town (and Why I Went Back)
paragraphs: Three years ago, I did something many of my friends in Bogotá talk about but never actually do. I gave up my apartment in Chapinero, packed my life into a small van and moved to a town of twelve thousand people in the coffee region. Last month, I moved back. People keep asking me which life is better. The honest answer is that both have disappointed me and both have surprised me.

Let me start with what I loved about the small town. The first thing I noticed was the time I suddenly had. In Bogotá, a sprawling city of nearly eight million people, I used to spend almost three hours a day in traffic. In the town, everything I needed was a ten-minute walk away. I could buy fresh fruit from a woman whose family had grown it for generations, and the man who repaired my shoes knew my name after a single visit.
There was also the silence, or rather the right kind of noise: birds at dawn, rain on a tin roof, church bells on Sunday. My blood pressure went down. I slept better than I had in a decade.

However, small-town life has its own pressures. Everybody knew everybody, which was lovely when I needed help and less lovely when I wanted privacy. Opportunities were limited, too. Although I could work online, the internet connection failed whenever it rained, which in the coffee region is often. And while I made some warm, kind friends, I missed the variety of people I used to meet in the capital: artists, scientists, people from every corner of the country.

The city, for all its problems, is vibrant in a way a small town can never be. On a single street in Bogotá you can find a tiny Peruvian restaurant, an independent bookshop and a jazz bar that only opens on Thursdays. New cafés and galleries spring up every month. Even the chaos has a kind of energy that I eventually realised I needed.

So I came back. This time, though, I chose an apartment within walking distance of my office, and I spend most weekends somewhere green. Whereas before I lived as if the city were the whole world, now I treat it as one option among many.

My advice to anyone dreaming of escape? Do it, but don't expect a perfect life. A small town won't solve every problem, and a big city won't destroy you. What matters is knowing what you need, and being honest enough to change your mind.

4.title: Larks, Owls and the Tyranny of the 7 a.m. Class
paragraphs: If you have ever sat in an early-morning class feeling groggy while the person next to you seems wide awake, biology may be partly to blame. Scientists have known for decades that people differ in their natural sleep timing, or chronotype. Some of us are larks, who wake up easily and feel most alert before lunch. Others are owls, who struggle in the morning but come alive in the evening. Most people fall somewhere in between.

Our chronotype is controlled by an internal clock in the brain that runs on a cycle of roughly twenty-four hours. Light is its most important signal. After seeing bright light in the morning, the body reduces its production of melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy. When evening comes, melatonin rises again, preparing us to wind down and hit the sack. In owls, this whole process simply happens later.

Genes play a significant role, but age matters too. Young children tend to be early risers, which many tired parents will confirm. During adolescence, however, the internal clock shifts later by as much as two hours. This means that a teenager who can't fall asleep before midnight is not necessarily being lazy or rebellious. Having been forced out of bed at six, many teenagers are effectively trying to learn while their brains still think it is the middle of the night.

This has important consequences for schools. In Colombia, as in much of Latin America, many public secondary schools start classes at around six thirty in the morning, partly because buildings are shared between a morning and an afternoon shift. Studies in several countries have found that when schools start later, students tend to sleep longer, arrive more punctually and feel less sluggish during lessons. Some studies have also linked later start times to better grades, although the results vary.

Adults are affected as well. Many offices still assume that the most productive workers are those who arrive first. Yet an owl who is forced to power through an eight o'clock meeting may perform worse than a lark, not because they are less capable but because they are working against their own biology. Since remote and flexible work became more common, some companies have started to let employees choose their hours, provided that they complete their tasks and attend key meetings.

Can an owl become a lark? Only to a limited extent. Experts suggest getting morning light, avoiding screens before bed and keeping a regular schedule, even at weekends. These habits can move the internal clock earlier by an hour or so. But unless society becomes more flexible, the owls of the world will probably keep feeling shattered every Monday morning.

4.title: The 3 a.m. Club
paragraphs: [This is an excerpt from Ritmo, a podcast about how people live and work. Hosts Camila and Julián are talking to Wilson Mena, who runs a bakery in Cali.]
CAMILA: Wilson, thanks for joining us. I understand you went to bed at what, seven last night?

WILSON: Seven thirty. I'm a creature of habit. I've hit the sack at the same time every night for fifteen years, unless there's a family party, and even then I leave early. My wife says I'm the most boring guest in Colombia.
JULIÁN: And you get up at…?

WILSON: Two forty-five. The alarm goes off, and I'm usually awake before it does. After washing my face and drinking a small coffee, I walk to the bakery. By three fifteen the ovens are on. We have to have pandebono and bread ready by six, because that's when the construction workers and the nurses from the night shift start coming in.
CAMILA: Honestly, I'd be shattered. Were you always a morning person?

WILSON: Not at all! As a teenager, I was a real night owl. I used to burn the midnight oil playing football in the street or listening to salsa on the radio, then I'd sleep in until noon on Saturdays. My mother despaired. When my uncle offered me a job in his bakery, I was nineteen, and the first month was terrible. I felt sluggish all day and fell asleep on the bus twice.
JULIÁN: So what changed?

WILSON: Mostly discipline. Since I couldn't change the bakery's hours, I had to change mine. I stopped drinking coffee after midday, and I made my bedroom completely dark. I also learned to take a short nap after lunch, but never more than twenty minutes, otherwise I wake up groggy.
CAMILA: What about your social life? Doesn't it suffer?

WILSON: Of course. I've missed concerts, weddings, football matches. That's the price. But I see my children every afternoon when they come home from school, which many parents who work office hours can't do. And there's something special about the city at four in the morning. While walking to work, I see the street sweepers, the taxi drivers finishing their shift, the first buses. We're a kind of secret club.
JULIÁN: Last question. Any advice for listeners who struggle to get up early?

WILSON: Be patient. Your body needs weeks, not days, to adjust. Go to bed at the same time every night, even on weekends, as long as you can. And find a reason to get up that matters to you. For me, it's the smell of bread coming out of the oven. Nothing in the world wakes you up faster.

5.title: Lost in (Polite) Translation
paragraphs: When Natalia Herrera moved from Bucaramanga to Hamburg to work as a civil engineer, she expected the language to be her biggest challenge. It wasn't. "My German was fine," she says. "What I wasn't ready for was how people talked to each other. In my first meeting, a colleague looked at my design and said, 'This won't work.' No introduction, no smile. I went to the bathroom and nearly cried."

Natalia's experience is extremely common among Latin Americans who work in northern Europe. Researchers who study workplace communication often describe cultures as falling somewhere on a scale between direct and indirect. In more direct cultures, it is considered efficient to get straight to the point, and people rarely mince their words, even with their bosses. In more indirect cultures, including much of Colombia, it is more important to protect the relationship, so criticism is softened, suggested or delivered through a third person.

Neither style is better, but problems arise when the two meet. To a German colleague, a Colombian who says "Maybe we could look at this again later" may seem vague or even dishonest. To a Colombian, a German who says "That's wrong" may come across as rude or arrogant. Both are simply following the rules they grew up with. The result is that people often talk at cross purposes, each convinced that the other is being difficult.

"Learning to read between the lines works in both directions," explains Marta Velasco, a Spanish-born consultant who trains international teams. "Northern Europeans need to understand that a Latin American 'yes, of course' may actually mean 'I have doubts'. And Latin Americans need to understand that a blunt comment usually isn't personal. It's about the work, not about you."

Velasco recommends that teams discuss these differences openly. Agreeing on some basic rules, for example that feedback will always be given in private, or that silence in a meeting does not mean agreement, can prevent many misunderstandings. Being aware of your own style, she adds, is the first step towards adapting it.

Three years later, Natalia says she has learned to enjoy the directness. "It's actually relaxing not to have to guess what people think," she says. "Nobody sugar-coats anything, so when my boss says my work is good, I know he means it." But on her visits home, she has noticed a new problem. "Last Christmas I told my aunt her tamal was a bit dry," she laughs. "It's not wise to be that candid with a Santandereana. She still hasn't forgiven me."

5.title: Dear Lucía: "My Colleague Keeps Talking Over Me"
paragraphs: Dear Lucía, I'm a 28-year-old marketing assistant at a medium-sized company in Barranquilla. I'm quite reserved by nature, and I've always preferred listening to talking. My problem is a colleague, Andrés, who is extremely outspoken. Every time I start to share an idea in a meeting, he talks over me. Sometimes he even repeats my idea five minutes later as if it were his own, and everyone congratulates him. I don't want to cause a scene, but I'm starting to feel invisible. My friends tell me to stop beating around the bush and confront him, but it's hard for me to be confrontational. What should I do? Silenced in Barranquilla

Dear Silenced, First of all, I want you to know that what you're describing is extremely common, and it isn't your fault. Being quiet is not a weakness. Many of the best ideas in any organisation come from people who think before they speak. The problem is not your personality but a meeting culture that rewards whoever talks loudest.
That said, it's important to protect your contributions, and there are ways to do it without turning into someone you're not. Here are a few strategies.

Prepare in advance. If you know the topic of a meeting, write down one or two points you want to make. It's much easier to speak up when you have a clear sentence ready. Sending a short email with your ideas before the meeting also creates a written record that they came from you.

Use a calm, polite phrase when you are interrupted. Something like "Sorry, Andrés, I'd just like to finish my point" is tactful but firm. You don't need to raise your voice. Saying it once, clearly, is usually enough.

Give credit to yourself, gently. If he repeats your idea, try: "Thanks, Andrés, that's exactly what I was suggesting earlier. Shall I explain how we could do it?" This isn't aggressive; it simply reminds everyone where the idea started.

Talk to him privately. It's possible that Andrés doesn't realise what he's doing. Some outspoken people genuinely don't read between the lines and need things explained directly. Choose a quiet moment and be candid: tell him how it makes you feel, focusing on specific situations rather than on his character.

Finally, if nothing changes, it's perfectly reasonable to mention the situation to your manager. Good managers want to hear from everyone, and they can make sure meetings are fair, for example by asking each person to speak in turn.
You don't need to become loud to be heard. You just need to be a little more strategic. Good luck! Lucía

6.title: The Hippo in the River: Anatomy of a Rumour
paragraphs: By nine o'clock on a Tuesday morning last August, almost everyone in the small riverside town of San Isidro had seen the video. It was only eleven seconds long and badly out of focus, but it appeared to show a large grey animal moving through the water near the bridge where children often swim. The message that came with it was alarming: "Hippo spotted in the river. Keep your kids at home!"

Colombia has a real hippo problem, of course. The animals that were brought illegally to the Magdalena Medio region in the 1980s have since multiplied into a population of well over a hundred, and they have occasionally been seen far from where they were first released. So the rumour didn't sound impossible. Within two hours, the local school had cancelled its swimming lessons, and two radio stations had broken the story without checking it.

Laura Pineda, a reporter for a regional news website, was more cautious. "I had been covering the hippo issue for three years, so I knew what they look like in the water," she says. "Something about the video seemed wrong. I decided to take it with a pinch of salt until I could get to the bottom of it."

Her first step was to find the original source. The video had been forwarded so many times that nobody knew who had filmed it. After several phone calls, she traced it to a fisherman who had recorded it on his phone the evening before. When she showed him the clip, he laughed. "That's my neighbour's cow," he told her. "She had escaped and was swimming across to the other side. I sent it to my cousin as a joke."

Pineda then tried to corroborate his account. She found two other eyewitnesses who had seen the cow in the river, and the neighbour confirmed that the animal had come home, wet and tired, later that night. A biologist who studied the video agreed that the shape of the head was clearly that of a cow.

By the time her article was published that afternoon, the story had been shared thousands of times. Some people were relieved; others refused to believe the explanation. One of the radio stations backtracked and apologised. The other has never corrected its report.

"What worries me is how quickly an unsubstantiated claim becomes 'news'," says Pineda. "The hippo issue is serious, and when stories like this are blown out of proportion, people stop trusting the real warnings. That's the most dangerous part."

6.title: Inside a Fact-Checking Newsroom
paragraphs: Andrea Molina has worked as a fact-checker in Bogotá for six years. Her small team checks claims made by politicians, viral posts and, increasingly, videos created with artificial intelligence. We spoke to her about how the job has changed.

Q: What does a typical day look like for you? A: There isn't really a typical day, which is part of the fun. This morning, for example, I've been checking a statistic that a senator used in a speech yesterday. I've already spoken to two economists and I've downloaded the official data, but I haven't reached a conclusion yet. Meanwhile, my colleagues have been tracking a rumour about a new tax that has been circulating on social media since the weekend.

Q: How has the job changed since you started? A: Enormously. When I started in 2020, most of the false content we saw was text: invented quotes, fake headlines. Over the last two years, we've seen a huge increase in manipulated images and audio. Last month we received a voice message that seemed to be from a famous footballer. It sounded completely real, but it had been created with an app.

Q: How do you decide what to check? A: We look at two things: how widely something has spread and how much harm it could cause. A silly story about a celebrity probably isn't worth our time. But a claim that a vaccine is dangerous, or that an election has been cancelled, can affect people's lives, so we prioritise those.

Q: What's the hardest part of your work? A: Honestly, it's the reaction. People often accuse us of being biased, whichever side the false claim came from. We've been insulted by supporters of every party. Our answer is to be transparent: we always publish our sources and explain exactly how we reached our verdict, so readers can check our work themselves.

Q: Have you ever got something wrong? A: Yes, twice. In both cases we published a correction at the top of the article and explained what had happened. Admitting a mistake quickly is essential if you want people to trust you.

Q: What advice would you give our readers? A: Before you share something, stop for ten seconds. Ask yourself who created it and why. If a story makes you very angry or very excited, that's exactly when you should be most careful. And if you can't find the same information on at least two reliable sites, it's better not to share it at all.

7.title: Isn't It Time We Read the Small Print?
paragraphs: We all click "I agree", don't we? A new app asks for permission to see our contacts, our location and our photos, and we accept without a second thought because we want to order lunch or edit a selfie. Studies suggest that almost nobody reads the terms and conditions. Honestly, who has the time? Some of these documents are longer than a short novel.

But isn't it strange that we accept rules we have never read, written by companies we have never met, about information that is deeply personal? Every time we search, like, buy or scroll, we add to our digital footprint. That data is being collected, analysed and sold right now, often to advertisers we have never heard of. It has been used to predict what we will buy, who we will vote for and even whether we are likely to become ill.

Defenders of the tech industry usually make two arguments. The first is that the services are free, so data is a fair price. The second is that users can always opt out. Neither argument convinces me. The services aren't really free if we are paying with our private lives. And opting out is often deliberately difficult: the button is hidden three menus deep, or refusing means the app simply stops working.

Some progress has been made. Colombia has had a data protection law since 2012, and the European Union's rules have forced companies around the world to ask for clearer consent. New regulations on artificial intelligence are being discussed in several countries, and stricter rules will probably be rolled out over the next few years. But laws only work if they are enforced, and if citizens know their rights.

Wouldn't it be better if privacy were the default setting rather than something we have to fight for? Imagine apps that collected only the information they actually needed, explained in two clear paragraphs what they would do with it, and deleted it after a reasonable time. That isn't a fantasy. Some companies already work this way, and they haven't gone out of business.

Until that becomes normal, we can take small steps. Check which apps can see your location. Delete the ones you no longer use. Read at least the summary of the privacy policy before you accept. None of this will make you invisible, but it will remind companies that we are paying attention.
Data privacy isn't only a technical issue, is it? It's about power: who has it, and who doesn't. The first step to getting some of it back is simply refusing to click "I agree" without thinking.

7.title: Seven Days Offline: A Classroom Experiment
paragraphs: When Mónica Arango, a social studies teacher at a public secondary school in Pereira, proposed that her tenth-grade students spend a week without social media, the reaction was immediate. "They looked at me as if I had asked them to stop breathing," she remembers. Eventually, twenty-six of her thirty-two students agreed to try. The rules were simple: phones could be used for calls, messages to family and schoolwork, but no social networks, no video platforms and no online games.

Before the experiment began, the students were asked to check their screen-time data. The results shocked many of them. The class average was just over six hours a day, and one student had spent more than eleven hours on his phone the previous Saturday. "I knew I was glued to my screen, but I didn't realise how much," said Sara, sixteen. "It was overwhelming to see the number."

The first two days were the hardest. Several students reported feeling anxious and bored, and many said they kept reaching for their phones without thinking. "It's addictive, isn't it? Your hand just goes to your pocket," explained Juan Diego. Three students gave up before Wednesday.

By the middle of the week, however, something had changed. Students said they were sleeping better and finding it easier to concentrate in class. Some rediscovered old hobbies: one girl finished a novel for the first time in two years, and a group of boys started playing football after school instead of watching videos of other people playing it. Several also noticed that they were less worried about keeping up with what their friends were posting.

Not everything was positive. Some students felt left out because their friends in other classes were organising plans on social networks. Others complained that they missed important news and that school announcements were sometimes posted only on Instagram. "We can't just log off from the world," one student wrote in his reflection. "The world is online."

At the end of the week, the students discussed what they had learned. Most said they would not delete their accounts, but twenty of them decided to set daily limits. Several also said they had become more aware of misinformation and echo chambers, having noticed how different the news felt when it wasn't filtered through their feeds.

Since the experiment, the idea has been copied by two other teachers at the school, and a version for parents is being planned for next term. "I didn't want to tell them technology is bad," says Arango. "I wanted them to decide for themselves how much of their attention they're willing to give away."

8.title: It's on the Tip of My Tongue!
paragraphs: You meet an old classmate in the supermarket. You remember where she sat, the colour of her school bag and the name of her dog, but her name? Nothing. You rack your brains, it begins with an M, maybe, and you feel it is right there, on the tip of your tongue. Then, two hours later, while you are washing the dishes, it suddenly appears: Marcela. Of course.

Psychologists call this a tip-of-the-tongue state, and it is one of the most common memory experiences in the world. Studies suggest that most adults have them about once a week, and that they become more frequent with age, which helps explain why grandparents so often call their grandchildren by the wrong name. Interestingly, people experiencing these moments can usually recall information related to the word, such as its first letter or number of syllables, even when the word itself refuses to come.

Why are names so difficult? One explanation is that names are arbitrary. The word 'baker' tells you something about the person; the name 'Marcela' tells you nothing. Researchers believe that information connected to many other ideas is easier to retrieve, because there are more paths leading to it. A name, linked only to a face, has very few paths. If one of them is blocked, you draw a blank.

Stress makes the problem worse, which is why students sometimes forget answers they knew perfectly well the night before. Under pressure, the brain releases hormones that interfere with the process of retrieval. That is also why trying harder rarely works. The more you concentrate on the missing word, the more you may activate a wrong one, which then gets in the way.

So what can you do? Experts suggest relaxing and thinking about something else. Going through the alphabet slowly can also jog your memory. And when you learn a new name, you can make it easier to remember later by connecting it to something vivid: imagine Marcela holding a giant mango, for example, or repeat the name aloud in conversation.

There is some good news, too. Most researchers agree that tip-of-the-tongue moments are not a sign of serious memory loss. In fact, they show that the memory is still there, stored safely in your brain. The connection has simply become a little slow. Being absent-minded now and then is completely normal. So next time a name slips your mind, don't panic. Go and wash the dishes.

8.title: The Woman Who Remembers Everything (Almost)
paragraphs: Valentina Gómez can memorise the order of a shuffled deck of 52 cards in under two minutes. She can recite a list of a hundred random words she heard only once, and she once memorised the phone numbers of every member of her extended family, all forty-three of them, as a birthday present for her grandmother. Yet she insists that she was born with a perfectly ordinary memory.

"At school I was the absent-minded one," says the 27-year-old psychology graduate from Manizales. "I'd forget my homework, my keys, my friends' birthdays. Things my teachers explained in class just didn't sink in." Everything changed at university, when a lecturer mentioned a technique used by ancient Greek speakers to remember long speeches. Intrigued, Valentina went home and started practising that same night.

The technique is known as the memory palace. You imagine a building you know well, such as your childhood home, and you 'place' each item you want to remember in a different location along a familiar route. To recall the information, you simply walk through the building in your mind. "The trick is to make each image as strange and vivid as possible," she explains. "If I need to remember 'bananas', I don't just imagine bananas on the table. I imagine a banana singing vallenato in my grandmother's kitchen. The brain loves absurd things."

After two years of training, Valentina entered her first national memory competition and came fourth. Since then she has competed in Mexico and Spain, and she now holds several Colombian records, which she admits is less impressive than it sounds. "There aren't many of us," she laughs. "But the community is growing."

What interests her most, however, is not competition but education. She now runs workshops for secondary school students who struggle with exams. "Many young people think they're bad at studying when really nobody has taught them how memory works," she says. "Once they grasp a few basic principles, their retention improves enormously." Her advice includes testing yourself instead of just rereading notes, and spacing out study sessions over several days.

Does she ever forget things now? "All the time," she says, smiling. "The techniques only work when I decide to use them. Last week I left my phone in a taxi. I can remember a thousand digits of pi, but I still have to mull over where I put my glasses every morning." Having a knack for memory, it seems, doesn't make anyone perfect.

9.title: Are Stereotypes Ever Useful?
paragraphs: Colombians are always late. The British are reserved. Argentinians talk about themselves. Most of us have heard statements like these, and many of us have repeated them, often as a joke. But are generalisations about national character ever useful, or do they always do more harm than good?

Supporters of generalisations argue that they are a natural part of how the human brain works. We cannot treat every situation as completely new, so we create categories to help us predict what will happen. In this sense, some cultural generalisations can be helpful. A Colombian businesswoman preparing for her first meeting in Tokyo would be wise to learn that, by and large, Japanese business culture values punctuality, formal greetings and indirect criticism. Knowing these norms may help her avoid embarrassing mistakes and fit in more quickly.

However, there is an important difference between a generalisation and a stereotype. A generalisation describes a tendency and accepts exceptions: 'Many people in this country prefer to eat dinner late.' A stereotype, on the other hand, paints an entire group with a broad brush and assumes that every individual is the same: 'They are all lazy.' Generalisations can be tested and changed when new information appears. Stereotypes, unlike generalisations, tend to resist evidence, especially when they are deep-rooted.

The danger of stereotypes is not only that they are inaccurate. They can also have real consequences. Colombians who travel abroad know this well. Despite the country's enormous cultural diversity, many of them have experienced jokes, suspicion or extra searches at airports because of images created by films and television series. Research also suggests that people who are constantly exposed to negative stereotypes about their group may perform worse in tests, a phenomenon psychologists call 'stereotype threat'.

Furthermore, generalisations about a nation hide the variety within it. Apart from a shared language and some customs, a fisherman from the Pacific coast, a student in Bogotá and a cattle farmer from the Llanos may have little in common. Their upbringing, music, food and even ways of speaking can be very different. Treating them as one 'typical Colombian' tells us almost nothing.

In conclusion, cultural generalisations can be useful starting points, provided we remember that they describe tendencies, not people. The problem begins when we stop observing and start assuming. Rather than asking people to conform to our expectations, we should let them surprise us, which, in my experience, they almost always do.

9.title: Summers in Two Languages
paragraphs: When I was a child, I used to live two lives. From September to June, I was Daniela, a quiet girl in a public school in New Jersey who ate peanut butter sandwiches and said "excuse me" every time she walked past someone. Every July, my parents would put my brother and me on a plane to Cali, and I would turn into "la gringuita", the cousin who spoke Spanish with a funny accent and didn't know how to dance salsa.

My grandmother's house in the neighbourhood of San Antonio was always full of people. Aunts and uncles would drop by without calling, neighbours would sit on plastic chairs outside the door until late, and nobody ever seemed to be alone. At first, it overwhelmed me. In New Jersey, you didn't visit someone without an invitation, and the street outside our house was silent after eight o'clock. In Cali, silence was considered almost rude.

I remember my first summer clearly. I was seven, and I didn't fit in at all. My cousins would laugh when I said "permiso" too formally, or when I refused to eat the chontaduro my uncle bought from a street seller. I used to cry at night because I wanted to go home. But by the end of August, I didn't want to leave. I had learned to dance, more or less, and my grandmother had taught me to make aborrajados, which I still cook for my own children today.

Back in the US, I would try to explain my other life to my friends, but it was hard. They imagined something from the news, not a grandmother who prayed the rosary every evening and kept a parrot that insulted the neighbours. I started to realise how little most people understood about where my family came from, and how easily they generalised.

Growing up between two cultures has shaped my whole life. I used to think I had to choose: was I American or Colombian? Now I know that this was the wrong question. I have the punctuality of New Jersey, except when I'm in Colombia, and the warmth of Cali, except, perhaps, in December, when I miss the cold.

My grandmother died three years ago. The house in San Antonio has been sold, and my cousins are scattered around the world. But every time I hear a salsa song from the seventies, I'm seven years old again, standing in her kitchen, learning to belong in two places at once.

10.title: How to Complain (and Actually Get Results)
paragraphs: Most of us put up with far more than we should. The internet company that charges us for a service we cancelled, the shoes that fall apart after a month, the restaurant that brings the wrong dish for the second time. We grumble to our friends, but we rarely complain to the people who could actually fix the problem. Often we don't want to make a fuss, or we simply don't know how. Here is a step-by-step guide.

1. Know your rights. In Colombia, the Consumer Protection Statute gives buyers the right to a legal guarantee, which means that a faulty product must be repaired, replaced or, in some cases, refunded. Shops are not allowed to tell you that it is "not their problem" and send you directly to the manufacturer.

2. Keep evidence. Save receipts, take photos of the damage and write down the dates and names of the people you speak to. If you complain by phone, ask for a reference number. What usually wins a dispute is not who shouts loudest but who has the best records.

3. Be clear about what you want. Before you contact the company, decide exactly what would solve the problem: a refund, a replacement, a discount or simply an apology. Companies find it much easier to respond when the request is specific.

4. Stay polite but firm. It is completely natural to feel angry, but aggression rarely helps. Indirect questions are your best friend here. Instead of "Why haven't you fixed this?", try "Could you tell me why the repair is taking so long?" or "I was wondering whether you could offer a replacement." These sound reasonable, but they still make it clear that you expect an answer.

5. Escalate if necessary. If the person you are talking to can't help, ask to take the matter up with a supervisor. If that fails, put your complaint in writing. Many companies are required to respond to formal complaints within fifteen working days. And if you still receive no answer, you can file a complaint with the Superintendence of Industry and Commerce, the government body that protects consumers.

6. Know when to accept an offer. Sometimes a company will offer a goodwill gesture, such as a voucher or a free month of service, even if it doesn't admit any fault. If this solves your problem, it may be worth accepting. If it doesn't, stand your ground and explain politely why it isn't enough.
Complaining well is a skill that improves with practice. The next time something goes wrong, don't wait until you're at the end of your tether. Act early, calmly and with your evidence ready.

10.title: The Fridge That Wouldn't Stay Cold
paragraphs: The fridge was the last straw. Before that, Hernando Peña had put up with a great deal: a delivery that arrived four days late, two technicians who never turned up, and a customer service line that played the same song for forty minutes. But when his brand-new fridge stopped working for the third time in two months, and he lost a whole week's shopping, including the fish his sister had brought him from Tumaco, he decided enough was enough.

"I have a bone to pick with you," he told the young woman who finally answered the phone. Then he stopped. He had been a schoolteacher for thirty years, and he knew that shouting rarely worked. He took a deep breath. "I'm sorry. It isn't your fault. Could you tell me who is responsible for warranty repairs in Bucaramanga?"

The woman, whose name was Yesenia, seemed surprised by his politeness. She explained that the repairs were handled by an external company, which was why the technicians kept missing appointments. "I was wondering whether it would be possible to replace the fridge instead," Hernando said. "This is the third time it has failed, and I have the receipts for every visit."

Yesenia said she didn't know whether that was allowed, but she promised to take it up with her supervisor. Hernando asked for a reference number and wrote it in the small notebook where he had recorded every date, every name and every broken promise.

Two days passed without an answer. Hernando wrote a formal email. He described the problem clearly, attached photos of the warm milk and the receipts, and explained exactly what he wanted: a new fridge, delivered and installed, plus compensation for the spoiled food. He ended with a sentence his daughter, a lawyer, had suggested: "If I do not receive a satisfactory response within fifteen working days, I will present my case to the relevant authority."

The reply arrived the next morning. The company apologised for "the inconvenience", offered a new fridge from a higher range, and, as a goodwill gesture, a gift voucher for a local supermarket. It wasn't exactly the redress he had asked for, since nothing could replace his sister's fish, but it was more than fair.

When the new fridge arrived, the delivery man asked him how he had managed it. "Everybody shouts at them," he said. "Nobody gets anything." Hernando smiled. "What I've learned," he said, "is that patience and paperwork are more powerful than anger." Then he went to the market to buy fish.

11.title: What Would You Do With a Lost Wallet?
paragraphs: Imagine you are working at the reception desk of a hotel when a stranger hands you a wallet. "I found this on the street," he says. "I'm in a hurry. Could you deal with it?" Then he leaves. Inside there is a key, a shopping list, a business card with an email address and some cash. What would you do? Would you contact the owner? And would it make a difference if there were more money inside?

A few years ago, a team of economists decided to find out. Over two years, research assistants 'lost' more than 17,000 wallets in hundreds of cities in forty countries, handing them in at banks, hotels, post offices and police stations. Some wallets contained no money; others contained the equivalent of about thirteen US dollars. In a smaller follow-up, some contained much more. The researchers then simply waited to see how many people would email the owner.

Most people, including the experts the team consulted beforehand, expected that more money would mean fewer returns. If you found a wallet full of cash, surely the temptation would be greater? The results suggested the opposite. In almost every country, wallets with money were returned more often than empty ones, and wallets with large amounts were returned most often of all.

Why? The researchers concluded that most people have a strong moral compass and a powerful wish to see themselves as honest. Keeping a wallet with no money feels like a minor mistake. Keeping one full of cash feels like theft, and most people draw the line there. Interestingly, wallets that contained a key were returned more often too, which suggests people were thinking about the owner's problem, not just their own reputation.

Return rates did vary a lot between countries, and the researchers warned against using the results to paint whole nations as honest or dishonest. Factors such as trust in institutions and the quality of the postal system probably played a role. The experiment also measured only one situation; honesty at a hotel desk may not predict honesty in politics or business.

Still, the study offers a hopeful message. We often assume that other people would behave badly if they had the chance. In reality, many people have qualms about taking what isn't theirs, even when nobody is watching. If we trusted each other a little more, perhaps we would design better systems, with fewer rules based on the idea that everyone is a potential thief.
So, back to the hotel desk. If that wallet were handed to you tomorrow, what would you do? Most people, it seems, would do the right thing.

11.title: The Spreadsheet
paragraphs: It was almost seven on a Friday evening when Camilo's manager called him into her office. Most of the accounting team had already left, and the only sound on the fourteenth floor was the cleaner's vacuum. Doña Patricia closed the door behind him and smiled in a way that made him nervous.

"I need a small favour," she said. "The quarterly report goes to the investors on Monday. The numbers are a bit disappointing, so I'd like you to move some of next quarter's sales into this one. It's just a question of timing. Everybody does it."

Camilo had been working at the firm for only eight months. It was his first real job after university, and he was proud of it. His mother told everyone in their neighbourhood in Soacha that her son worked in an office with a view of the mountains. He knew exactly what Patricia was asking for, and he knew it wasn't legal.
"Can I think about it over the weekend?" he asked.
"Of course," she said. "But I'll need it by Sunday night."

He didn't sleep much that weekend. On Saturday, he tried to persuade himself that it wasn't so serious. If he refused, she would probably ask someone else, and he would lose his job for nothing. If he agreed, nobody would ever find out. But every time he opened the spreadsheet, he had second thoughts. He kept thinking about his father, a bus driver who had once spent an entire afternoon looking for a passenger to return a forgotten phone. "Integrity is what you do when nobody is watching," his father used to say.

On Sunday evening, Camilo sent Patricia a short, polite email. He said he wasn't comfortable changing the figures and suggested they present the real numbers with a clear explanation. He attached a draft of that explanation. Then he turned off his phone.

On Monday, Patricia didn't mention the email. The report went out with the original figures. Two months later, an internal audit discovered that another department had manipulated its accounts, and three managers were dismissed. Patricia was not one of them, but she was moved to a different office soon afterwards.

Camilo still works at the firm. Sometimes he wishes he had refused immediately, on that Friday evening, instead of asking for time. "If only I had been braver," he says. "But I'm glad I stood up for what I believed in. I wouldn't want to have a career that I couldn't explain to my father."

12.title: Six Months in Montreal: What Nobody Told Me
paragraphs: When I landed in Montreal last January, it was minus twenty-four degrees outside. I was wearing the warmest jacket I could find in Bogotá, which turned out to be completely useless. As I waited for a taxi, my eyelashes started to freeze. I remember thinking: what have I done?
Six months later, I'm still here, and I've learned a lot. So for anyone thinking about a fresh start abroad, here are the things nobody told me before I left.

Culture shock comes in waves. The first few weeks were exciting. Everything was new: the snow, the bagels, the way people say "bonjour-hi" in shops. Then, around the second month, the excitement disappeared, and I was suddenly, painfully homesick. I missed my mother's ajiaco, the noise of my neighbourhood, even the traffic on the Séptima. I cried in a supermarket because I couldn't find arepas that tasted right. Experts say this is completely normal, and that it passes. For me, it did, but slowly.

Red tape is real, everywhere. I had imagined that bureaucracy was a Colombian speciality. It isn't. Getting my health card, opening a bank account and finding an apartment without a local credit history took weeks of forms, waiting rooms and confused phone calls in my imperfect French.

Language is about more than grammar. I had studied French for two years, and I could pass exams. But on my first day at work, I felt like a fish out of water. Quebec French has its own vocabulary and rhythm, and my colleagues switched between French and English in the same sentence. If I hadn't joined a conversation group at the local library, I would still be nodding and smiling without understanding anything.

Small routines help you settle in. Learning to get around on the metro, finding a café where the waiter knows my order, joining a Sunday football team with other Latin Americans: these small things made the city feel like home. Nobody tells you how important they are.

Would I do it again? Absolutely. Living here has broadened my horizons in ways I couldn't have imagined. If I had stayed in my comfortable job in Bogotá, I wouldn't be the independent person I am now.

I don't know yet whether I'll put down roots here. But I have a plan. By this time next year, I will have finished my master's degree, and I will have been working at the engineering firm for eighteen months. And by then, I hope, I will have bought a proper winter coat.

12.title: Why Foreigners Are Putting Down Roots in Colombia
paragraphs: Not so long ago, Colombia was a country that people left. During the difficult decades of the late twentieth century, millions of Colombians moved to Venezuela, the United States and Spain in search of safety and work. Today the picture is more complicated. While many Colombians still emigrate, the country has also become a destination for people arriving from abroad.

The largest group by far comes from Venezuela. Since the economic crisis there deepened in the mid-2010s, close to three million Venezuelans have settled in Colombia, making it the main host country in the region. For many of them, the move was not a choice but a necessity. "When we crossed the border at Cúcuta, we had two suitcases and a baby," says Yolimar, a nurse who now lives in Barranquilla. "The hardest part was the red tape. Without papers, you can't work legally, you can't rent an apartment, you can't even open a bank account." Colombia's temporary protection status, introduced in 2021, has allowed well over a million people to regularise their situation.

A very different group has also grown quickly: remote workers and retirees from North America and Europe. Attracted by the climate, the relatively low cost of living and the warmth of the people, many have chosen cities like Medellín, Santa Marta and Bogotá. Klaus, a retired engineer from Hamburg, moved to Santa Marta four years ago. "In Germany, I'd be sitting at home watching the rain," he says. "Here I swim in the sea every morning."

Adapting is not always easy. Many newcomers report feeling like a fish out of water at first, particularly if they speak little Spanish. Klaus admits that it took him a year to acclimatise to the heat and to the idea that a meeting at three o'clock might begin at half past. "If I had been more patient at the beginning, I would have enjoyed that first year much more," he says.

The arrival of wealthier foreigners has also caused tension. In some neighbourhoods of Medellín, residents complain that short-term rentals have pushed up prices, forcing local families to move. City authorities are now discussing new regulations, which are expected to be introduced over the next few years.
